question.problem:
Let $X$ be a random variable with the probability density function shown below. What are the modes of $X?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{x}^{4}}{2}, & -1\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14158570/assets/4733d066bd04d8bbc7fb8203694452b84fd8000b1e616d7afcfad3351ce9e27d.svg)
current_example.worked_solution:
The modes of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ are the values of $x$ at the global maxima of $f(x).$

To find the global maxima of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $0 \leq x \leq 2$ is $f(x) = \dfrac{3}{2}(x-1)^2.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2(x-1) \\  & =3(x-1),\end{aligned}
$$

and solving $f'(x) = 0,$ we get

$$
3(x-1)= 0\quad \Longrightarrow \quad x=1.
$$

This critical point is within the interval $[0,2],$ so we keep it.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x = 0, 2.$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,1, 2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{3}{2}(0-1)^{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ f(1) & =\frac{3}{2}(1-1)^{2}=0 \\ f(2) & =\frac{3}{2}(2-1)^{2}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest values are

$$
f(0 ) = f( 2) = \dfrac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the modes of $X$ are $0$ and $2.$
